title: Learning Mixture Models via Efficient High-dimensional Sparse Fourier Transforms
text: the sum-of-squares method for robust statistics [ kothari_outlier-robust_2017 , kothari_better_2017 , hopkins2018mixture ] that eventually led to the full resolution of the question [ bakshi2020outlier , bakshi2022robustly ] via connections to algorithmic properties related to verifying concentration and anti-concentration [ karmalkar_list-decodable_2019 , raghavendra_list_2019 ] of high-dimensional probability distributions. The main goal of this work is to introduce a new class of methods that apply to learning spherical (i.e., covariance ∝ I \propto I ) mixture models. To show the contrast with previous work and motivate our methods, we summarize three high-level conclusions that emerge from the above line of work: Minimum Separation. For learning the parameters of a mixture with k k components, all polynomial time/sample algorithms need a minimum Euclidean separation between the cluster means of γ = ( log ⁡ k ) \gamma=\Omega(\sqrt{\log k}) and this is provably necessary [ regev_learning_2017 ] . Moment-Based Methods. Virtually all known algorithms for parameter estimation in GMMs (from the work of [ pearson1894contributions ] to recent advances, e.g. , [ hopkins2018mixture , kothari2018robust , liu2022clustering ] ) fundamentally rely on algorithms that try to find clusters with low-degree empirical moments matching/behaving similarly to that of a Gaussian. Certifiably Bounded Distributions. Even the most general methods developed for learning mixture models only apply when the cluster distributions have sufficiently light tails and there is an efficiently verifiable certificate [ kothari_outlier-robust_2017 ] of this property. We know this is true for all sub-Gaussian distributions thanks to recent advances [ diakonikolas2024sos , kothari_better_2017 ]
